messages.body_plain:
Hi Eric

Yes, that is how predict.secr works. The base levels of covariates are those for the first observation in the dataset. When there are multiple covariates this is ensures that the prediction is done at a combination of levels that is in the data, rather than one that potentially lies outside.

It is definitely a trap for the unwary, and perhaps should be changed. Some tips that may help:
-- You can specify any levels you like in the 'newdata' argument of predict.secr, and this is the best route
--  If you are uncertain about the default levels, set the 'savenew' argument and inspect the resulting attribute (see code below)
-- To see how the default newdata is generated, try secr.make.newdata.

Murray

Example with ovenCH[[4]] in which the first individual is male (M) rather than female (F):

> fit <- secr.fit(ovenCH[[4]], CL = TRUE, model = g0~Sex, buffer = 250)

> pred <- predict(fit, savenew = TRUE)
> attr(pred, 'newdata')

messages.body_plain:
Dear secr community,

I am trying to estimate population densities for a neotropical rodent species that I captured in several independent sites and have a bunch of different questions. I hope the structure of my post (f.e. several unrelated questions at once) is allright. If you prefer independent posts for each topic please let me know!

1.Comparability between sites:
I would like to compare population densities for on species that was captured in different habitat types (we have several replicas per habitat type). Due to topography, size and form of habitat patches, it was difficult to standardize the trapping design for all habitat types. The distance between trapping stations was generally the same for all habitat types but the overall design differed between them: transect pairs or trapping grids.
My question is whether I will produce biased density estimates because the trapping design differs between habitat types.

2. Set start manually:
For most of my capture sites secr.fit works well with different model specifications
secrAS51 <- secr.fit (psemiCH.AS5, model = g0~1, mask = AS5.mask, method = "BFGS")
secrAS52 <- secr.fit (psemiCH.AS5, model = g0~b , mask = AS5.mask, method = "BFGS")
secrAS53 <- secr.fit (psemiCH.AS5, model = list(g0~b, sigma~b), mask = AS5.mask, method = "BFGS")
secrAS55 <- secr.fit (psemiCH.AS5, model = g0~b+T, mask = AS5.mask, method = "BFGS")

(the only model that almost never works out is g0 ~ h2; I used method = "BFGS" because it was resulting in much less error messages than either Newton-Raphson or Nelder-Mead )

For some sites secr.fit only works if I set the start manually. However, I am having doubts about specifiying the starting values for D, g0 and sigma. Can I infer these values from my capture data e.g. N of individuals divided by the area of the habitat mask as an approximation for D? For sigma I can imagine the minimum home range size as being a good starting point.

3. model average()
As mentioned above several models run well. For model.average() I read the recommendation based on Turek and Fletcher (2012) in the secr manual to use AIC instead of AICc. However, the SE estimate using criterion = AICc seems more "realistic" (I do not want to use the word "better") than the SE estimate that I get when using criterion = AIC (see below)

model.average(secrAS51, secrAS52, secrAS53, secrAS55, realnames = NULL, betanames = NULL,
alpha = 0.05, dmax = 10, covar = FALSE, average = "real",
criterion = "AIC", CImethod = "Wald")

        estimate SE.estimate          lcl         ucl
D      4.5839589  40.1277902  0.076827326 273.5052785
g0     0.0869694   0.1049543  0.007091151   0.5595572
sigma 28.5644831   6.3475692 18.575818476  43.9242930

for criterion = AICc
         estimate SE.estimate         lcl        ucl
D      2.35663989  0.89970741  1.14370613  4.8559253
g0     0.02611265  0.01029052  0.01198583  0.0559469
sigma 28.67187765  0.68973787 27.35157746 30.0559106

Any recommendations which criterion I should use?

Thank you very much for investing your time in reading this long post! I am greatful for any help!

All the best,
Julian

messages.body_plain:
Hello Julian, and welcome to the group

1. If your animals are behaving according to the model, and you have adequate data (not too sparse, traps not too far apart) then different trapping designs should all produce unbiased estimates. There is a potential problem with parallel transects if animals have home ranges elongated systematically in one direction with respect to the transects; elongation is almost certainly _not_ a problem with layouts that don't have a strong 'grain' (e.g., square grids). So there is a potential effect of layout on estimates in that case.

2. I'm surprised g0~h2 'almost never works' if you are using the default detection function detectfn = 0 or 'HN' - I wonder what causes that? Regarding start values: you are free to use whatever works for you. For sigma I suggest 0.2 times the sqrt of the home range area in sq. metres (or the home range radius / 2.5). The simplest form for the start values is a list of real parameter values like: start = list(D=1, g0=0.2, sigma=25). You may also find it convenient to pass the name of a previously fitted model (secr.fit will find the values it needs).

3. Something has gone seriously wrong with the model averaging using AIC (D-hat 4.6, SE 40.1!). Do you have a reason to override the default for 'average' (averaging on the link scale)? That is the scale on which the SE really 'make sense'. If the problem persists, and isn't just due to a really strange model, I'm going to have to look at the code, which may not happen for a few days.

Hope this is some use
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Checking Otis et al. (1978) p 120: their test is based on the distribution of Qi, the time between first and last
capture for the ith animal caught at least twice. In your case (2 occasions) all animals caught twice necessarily have Qi = 1, and there is no information on closure. My intuition is that it's impossible to dream up a closure test for 2 occasions. If you can get an electronic copy of Otis et al. (1978) it's worth searching for 'closure' - you will find many reservations about closure tests (their limited power and potential for responding to effects other than closure), that should be heeded, and the general note that their methods require >2 occasions.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jess,
A few comments:

I think the easiest way to test for closure violation within 90-day subsets of the total study duration would be to build the capthist object for the complete data set, then use subset.capthist() to divide the data into 4 separate data sets (not necessarily "sessions"), and then perform the test on each data set.

One of your error messages indicates that the number of usage fields doesn't match the number of occasions. As you split up your capture data, the associated trap file should have only the appropriate usage columns (e.g. for session 2 you would only include usage columns 91-180).  I think subset.capthist() would do this for you.

Note that if you test for closure within 90-day sessions and find no violation, then you can assume populations were closed within those 90-day sessions, but not that they were closed for the whole study period. If you plan to pool the data across all 367 days to estimate density, then you should test for closure across this whole time period.  Perhaps your supervisor was suggesting you divide the data into 4 sessions and estimate density separately for each (closed) session (perhaps using a robust design framework)?

I'm not sure if this is causing errors, but if you want to stick with "session", I think it would make sense to code your occasions as starting at occasion 1 within each session.

Good luck!
Eric

Hi Jess,
Switching to multimark might be useful to you in this case because of the left- and right-handed data, but won't solve the closure problem - all "closed-population" estimators, including those implemented in multimark, rely on the same assumption.  The tests for closure aren't perfect, and researchers often have to make the argument, based on the biology of the species or knowledge of the population sampled, that few additions or losses of individuals were likely to have occurred during sampling (e.g. because birth and death rates are low and dispersal is rare). I'll mention again that collapsing your data into longer occasions might help, and not just for the closure test, as very low occasion-specific capture probabilities might cause various methods to perform poorly.

Eric

Jessica

It seems to me that the closure.test() warning message is a poor reason to abandon 'secr' (of course there may be other good reasons to do so!) (i) the message you are bothered by is only a warning not to take the p value at face value, (ii) any such test probably has low power, and is subject to many qualifications (I included closure.test() in 'secr' as a curiosity, not because I thought anyone should use it), and (iii) population turnover (non-closure) will bias SECR estimates, but intuitively the bias is proportional to the magnitude of the turnover, and will often be swamped by sampling error. A test for closure cannot really resolve the question of whether non-closure is a problem - that requires biological judgement, and possibly simulation of scenarios involving turnover. If there is enough turnover to distort the estimates then there are strategies you can use in 'secr' to correct this, such as subdividing the analysis into 'sessions' while constraining density to be constant across sessions.

I make these general points to set the record straight on SECR and 'secr'; I'm not trying to persuade you to stick with them if other methods better fit your problem.

Murray
